title: Real-time closed-loop protocol to assess neural variability in temporal coding
summary: Understanding temporal coding in neural systems is essential for decoding brain communication and advancing knowledge of neural information processing. Neural activity often conveys information through spike sequences with stereotypical temporal structures linked to specific functions. However, these sequences are subject to variability introduced by neural dynamics. Real-time closed-loop stimulation is a powerful approach to study temporal coding through adaptive control. In this work, we evaluate how a closed-loop protocol adapts to this variability to drive neural dynamics toward a desired state. It computes the Victor-Purpura distance to quantify similarity between spike sequences generated by the neural system and a triggering pattern. If the protocol determines that a neural sequence is similar to the trigger pattern, it applies stimulation to the system. This allows for an analysis of whether the system's responses are consistent and facilitates the identification of varying spike sequences that can be considered instances of the same functional temporal code. We designed two validation experiments using the Hindmarsh-Rose model: (i) detection of a temporal code and delivery of stimulation to produce brief interspersed bursts, and (ii) detection of burst onset in chaotic activity followed by inhibitory stimulation to regularize it. Gaussian noise was progressively injected to increase variability. The protocol exhibited high degree of adaptability to variability and was effective in achieving the target dynamics. The results reported in this paper suggest that adaptive closed-loop stimulation can enhance experimental methodologies for studying neural coding under realistic variability conditions.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates a real-time closed-loop stimulation protocol that uses the Victor-Purpura distance to detect spike sequences similar to a triggering pattern and applies stimulation to drive neural dynamics toward desired states. Tested on the Hindmarsh-Rose model under progressively added Gaussian noise, the protocol showed high adaptability to variability and effectively achieved target dynamics, suggesting it can enhance experimental methods for studying temporal coding under realistic conditions.
AI.motivation: Understanding temporal coding is essential for decoding brain communication, but neural spike sequences exhibit variability introduced by neural dynamics. There is a need for methods that can study temporal coding despite this variability, motivating adaptive closed-loop stimulation approaches.
AI.method: A closed-loop protocol computes the Victor-Purpura distance to quantify similarity between spike sequences and a triggering pattern. When similarity is detected, stimulation is applied. Two validation experiments were designed using the Hindmarsh-Rose model: (i) detecting a temporal code and delivering stimulation to produce brief interspersed bursts, and (ii) detecting burst onset in chaotic activity followed by inhibitory stimulation to regularize it. Gaussian noise was progressively injected to increase variability.
AI.result: The closed-loop protocol exhibited a high degree of adaptability to variability and was effective in achieving the target dynamics in both validation experiments, even as Gaussian noise was progressively increased.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive closed-loop stimulation can enhance experimental methodologies for studying neural coding under realistic variability conditions, providing a way to identify varying spike sequences that represent instances of the same functional temporal code.

title: Beyond Tokens: Probing Higher-Order Epistasis in Learned Protein Representations
summary:
Protein fitness landscapes contain nonlinear interactions in which mutation effects depend on other residues. We introduce ORBIT, an Order-Resolved Benchmarking of Interaction Transformations framework that separates interaction presence, representation accessibility, and functional recovery. ORBIT first validates Walsh-based diagnostics on synthetic landscapes with known interaction order, then analyzes the experimentally measured GB1 fitness landscape under the FLIP 2-vs-rest setting. We compare ridge regression, a standard MLP, independent tokens, nonlinear independent tokens, and Residual Interaction Tokenization (RIT).
  Across 20 paired training seeds, the primary two-hidden-layer comparison found no significant architecture differences in FLIP test R^2, third- or fourth-order functional recovery, or final-layer third- or fourth-order accessibility. However, RIT significantly increased pairwise accessibility at the token stage relative to both independent-token controls (Delta A_tok,2 = 0.2468, d_z = 1.67, Holm-adjusted p = 1.14 x 10^-5), without a detectable downstream higher-order advantage.
  A pre-specified depth/capacity analysis showed that deeper MLPs improved FLIP prediction, third-order functional recovery, and final-layer third-order accessibility; fourth-order accessibility also improved relative to the shallow MLP but remained below zero in absolute held-out R^2. ORBIT therefore reveals representation-level changes hidden by conventional prediction metrics and distinguishes early interaction-aware encoding from higher-order structure constructed by downstream nonlinear capacity.

AI.tldr: ORBIT is a benchmarking framework that separates interaction presence, representation accessibility, and functional recovery in protein fitness landscapes. Applied to the GB1 fitness landscape, it shows that while architectures perform similarly on standard prediction metrics, RIT specifically increases pairwise interaction accessibility at the token stage, while deeper networks improve higher-order recovery through downstream nonlinear capacity.
AI.motivation: Protein fitness landscapes contain nonlinear interactions where mutation effects depend on other residues, but conventional prediction metrics may hide representation-level differences in how models encode these interactions.
AI.method: ORBIT uses Walsh-based diagnostics validated on synthetic landscapes with known interaction order, then analyzes the experimentally measured GB1 fitness landscape under the FLIP 2-vs-rest setting, comparing ridge regression, standard MLP, independent tokens, nonlinear independent tokens, and Residual Interaction Tokenization (RIT) across 20 paired training seeds with pre-specified depth/capacity analyses.
AI.result: No significant architecture differences in FLIP test R^2 or higher-order functional recovery, but RIT significantly increased pairwise accessibility at the token stage (Delta A_tok,2 = 0.2468, d_z = 1.67, p = 1.14 x 10^-5). Deeper MLPs improved prediction, third-order functional recovery, and accessibility, though fourth-order accessibility remained below zero.
AI.conclusion: ORBIT reveals representation-level changes hidden by conventional prediction metrics, distinguishing early interaction-aware encoding from higher-order structure constructed by downstream nonlinear capacity.

title: A meta-algorithm for ab initio reconstruction of complex mixtures in cryo-EM
summary: We describe a systematic approach for spawning and aggregating multi-class cryo-EM reconstruction jobs. This approach formalizes standard ad hoc strategies of iterative classification and filtering typically used by practitioners to sort impure, heterogeneous samples. To our knowledge, this is the first method that can successfully perform ab initio reconstruction on datasets containing dozens of distinct species. We obtain 97% accuracy on ab initio reconstruction of a 45-class subset of Tomotwin-100, 75% accuracy on the full Tomotwin-100 dataset, and demonstrate recovery of ribosomal assembly states from an unfiltered experimental cryo-EM dataset. Our approach's capability scales with compute and lays the foundation for automated cryo-EM workflows in modern experimental settings.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a systematic framework for spawning and aggregating multi-class cryo-EM reconstruction jobs, enabling ab initio reconstruction on datasets containing dozens of distinct species. It achieves 97% accuracy on a 45-class subset and 75% accuracy on the full Tomotwin-100 dataset, plus demonstrates recovery of ribosomal assembly states from an unfiltered experimental dataset.
AI.motivation: Standard cryo-EM workflows rely on ad hoc iterative classification and filtering strategies to handle impure, heterogeneous samples, which are not systematic or scalable. There is a need for a formalized approach that can handle datasets containing dozens of distinct species for ab initio reconstruction.
AI.method: The approach formalizes standard practices of iterative classification and filtering into a systematic framework for spawning (launching) and aggregating (merging) multi-class reconstruction jobs across heterogeneous cryo-EM datasets.
AI.result: The method achieves 97% accuracy on a 45-class subset of Tomotwin-100, 75% accuracy on the full Tomotwin-100 dataset, and successfully recovers ribosomal assembly states from an unfiltered experimental cryo-EM dataset.
AI.conclusion: This approach's capability scales with computational resources and provides a foundation for automated cryo-EM workflows in modern experimental settings, representing the first method capable of ab initio reconstruction on datasets containing dozens of distinct species.

title: Propensity Straight-Through Gradients for Discrete Stochastic Systems
summary: Continuous-time Markov chains (CTMCs) provide the backbone for modeling discrete stochastic dynamics across applied, physical, and biological sciences. Their integration with modern gradient-based machine learning, however, is limited by the hard categorical event selection intrinsic to Gillespie-type simulation algorithms. We exploit the affine state update to obtain the exact one-step conditional-mean sensitivity by differentiating normalized reaction propensities. We pair this backward rule with exact forward trajectories to define the propensity straight-through (PST) estimator. At the trajectory level, we show that one-step sensitivities composed across events can depart from the exact multistep sensitivity. We derive the resulting per-step discrepancy in closed form and prove that it vanishes identically for affine downstream dependence. PST matches the accuracy of Gumbel-Softmax straight-through across all benchmarks: reversible dimerization (0.06% error), a genetic oscillator (1.7% error), a 50-task repressilator suite (0.17% median error), and patch-clamp ion-channel recordings ($R^2$ = 0.988). Under matched settings, PST converges 3.0-fold faster on the oscillator and 2.1-fold faster on the ion channel. At deep-learning scale, PST trains a 203,796-parameter stochastic reaction network with hard sampling, reaching 98.22% MNIST digit classification accuracy. By differentiating an exact conditional mean rather than a relaxed sample, PST offers a temperature- and Gumbel-free path to scalable gradient-based learning through exact stochastic trajectories.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the propensity straight-through (PST) estimator, a gradient estimation method for continuous-time Markov chains (CTMCs) that differentiates exact conditional-mean sensitivities rather than relaxed samples, enabling scalable gradient-based learning through exact stochastic trajectories without temperature or Gumbel noise.
AI.motivation: CTMCs are fundamental for modeling discrete stochastic dynamics across many scientific fields, but integrating them with gradient-based machine learning is limited by the hard categorical event selection in Gillespie-type simulation algorithms, which blocks differentiable pathways.
AI.method: The authors exploit the affine state update to obtain exact one-step conditional-mean sensitivity by differentiating normalized reaction propensities, combining this backward rule with exact forward trajectories to define the PST estimator. They derive the per-step discrepancy in closed form and prove it vanishes for affine downstream dependence.
AI.result: PST matches Gumbel-Softmax straight-through accuracy across benchmarks (reversible dimerization 0.06% error, genetic oscillator 1.7%, repressilator suite 0.17% median, patch-clamp ion channels R²=0.988), converges 3.0x faster on the oscillator and 2.1x faster on ion channels, and trains a 203,796-parameter stochastic reaction network reaching 98.22% MNIST accuracy.
AI.conclusion: By differentiating an exact conditional mean rather than a relaxed sample, PST offers a temperature- and Gumbel-free path to scalable gradient-based learning through exact stochastic trajectories, providing both accuracy and computational efficiency advantages.

title: A spinal circuit for collective coordination
comment: Main text (26 pages), 5 Figures, Supplementary materials (15 pages)
summary: The coordinated movement of animal groups is one of the most widespread social behaviors, which are generally attributed to high-order cognitive processing in the brain. Yet, collective coordination can seemingly emerge from rapid, local interactions between individuals, suggesting the existence of decentralized mechanisms of online coordination that remain to be identified. Here, we show that a low-order spinal sensorimotor circuit is required for real-time social coordination during schooling in zebrafish. Central to this circuit are intraspinal proprioceptive neurons that detect local body bending and deliver direct, curvature-based inhibition to precisely time the locomotor network. Combining electrophysiology, calcium imaging, optogenetics, and behavioral analysis, we show that this circuit encodes both self-generated (egocentric) and neighbor-induced (allocentric) body bending signals, enabling fish to match the phase of their swimming to the wakes of their neighbors (vortex phase matching). In a neuromechanical model and physical robot, this single feedback loop is sufficient to generate vortex phase matching and to lower the energetic cost of swimming. Disrupting this circuit uncouples neighboring fish and abolishes schooling behavior. These results show that a spinal circuit dynamically synchronizes individuals through simple, local interactions, revealing how low-order mechanisms can drive the emergence of coordinated group behavior.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies a low-order spinal sensorimotor circuit in zebrafish that enables real-time social coordination during schooling. Intraspinal proprioceptive neurons detect both self-generated and neighbor-induced body bending, delivering curvature-based inhibition to the locomotor network, which allows fish to match their swimming phase to neighbors' wakes. The circuit is sufficient for vortex phase matching and energetic savings, and when disrupted, schooling behavior is abolished.
AI.motivation: Coordinated animal group movement is traditionally attributed to brain-level cognitive processing. However, evidence suggests collective coordination may emerge from rapid, local interactions between individuals, pointing to the existence of unidentified decentralized mechanisms for online coordination. The authors aim to uncover these low-order mechanisms.
AI.method: The authors combine electrophysiology, calcium imaging, optogenetics, and behavioral analysis to characterize a spinal sensorimotor circuit. They also validate findings using a neuromechanical model and a physical robot to test whether a single feedback loop is sufficient to generate vortex phase matching and energetic benefits.
AI.result: The intraspinal proprioceptive neurons encode both egocentric (self-generated) and allocentric (neighbor-induced) body bending signals, and deliver curvature-based inhibition to precisely time the locomotor network. This enables vortex phase matching, reduces swimming energy costs, and disrupting the circuit uncouples neighboring fish and abolishes schooling.
AI.conclusion: A spinal circuit dynamically synchronizes individuals through simple local interactions, demonstrating that low-order sensorimotor mechanisms can drive the emergence of coordinated group behavior. This challenges the assumption that collective coordination requires high-order brain processing.

title: What sets the critical genome length for sympatric speciation? A closed form and asymptotic theory
summary: In the Derrida--Higgs model of sympatric speciation, a sexually reproducing population with finite binary genomes can mate only when the genetic overlap between two individuals exceeds a threshold $q_{\min}$. Depending on the genome length $L$, the population either remains genetically connected or fragments into reproductively isolated species. A central problem is therefore to predict the critical genome length $L_c$ at which fragmentation begins. At finite $L$, fluctuations broaden the overlap distribution and allow genetically distant regions of the population to remain connected. A previously proposed transient variance criterion captures this effect, but its evaluation requires numerical iteration of coupled moment equations. Here we first correct the unrestricted moment equations by removing a previously implicit assumption and then derive an explicit closed form expression for $L_c$. The resulting formula shows that the critical genome length is determined, at the time the mean overlap reaches $q_{\min}$, by the competition between deterministic separation from the unrestricted equilibrium and the transient genealogical variance of the overlap distribution. This expression permits a systematic asymptotic analysis. When the deterministic contribution dominates, $L_c$ becomes essentially independent of the population size $M$ and scales as $μ^{-2}$. When the transient genealogical variance dominates, $L_c$ grows as $M^{3/2}$ or as $\sqrt{M}/μ$, depending on how $M$ and the mutation rate $μ$ jointly vary. Simulations support all predicted behaviors. Our results identify transient genealogical variance as the principal mechanism linking finite genome fluctuations to the onset of reproductive fragmentation and provide a practical analytical prediction for the critical genome length.

AI.tldr: The paper derives an explicit closed-form expression for the critical genome length L_c in the Derrida-Higgs sympatric speciation model, correcting previous moment equations and showing that L_c is determined by competition between deterministic separation from the unrestricted equilibrium and transient genealogical variance. The formula enables asymptotic analysis revealing distinct scaling regimes (μ^-2, M^3/2, or √M/μ) depending on parameter dominance, all confirmed by simulations.
AI.motivation: Predicting the critical genome length L_c at which a sexually reproducing population fragments into reproductively isolated species in the Derrida-Higgs model. Prior approaches required numerical iteration of coupled moment equations, and there was an implicit assumption error in the unrestricted moment equations that needed correction.
AI.method: The authors correct the unrestricted moment equations by removing a previously implicit assumption, then derive an explicit closed-form expression for L_c. The expression captures the competition between deterministic separation from the unrestricted equilibrium and transient genealogical variance at the time the mean overlap reaches q_min. This enables systematic asymptotic analysis across different parameter regimes.
AI.result: The closed-form expression shows L_c varies by regime: when deterministic contribution dominates, L_c is essentially independent of population size M and scales as μ^-2; when transient genealogical variance dominates, L_c scales as M^3/2 or √M/μ depending on how M and μ jointly vary. Simulations confirm all predicted scaling behaviors.
AI.conclusion: Transient genealogical variance is identified as the principal mechanism linking finite genome fluctuations to the onset of reproductive fragmentation. The work provides a practical analytical prediction for L_c and corrects the underlying moment equations of the model.

title: Evaluating Post-hoc Explanations of the Transformer-based Genome Language Model DNABERT-2
comment: Accepted at the 4th World Conference on Explainable Artificial Intelligence, XAI-2026
summary: Explaining deep neural network predictions on genome sequences enables biological insight and hypothesis generation-often of greater interest than predictive performance alone. While explanations of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have been shown to capture relevant patterns in genome sequences, it is unclear whether this transfers to more expressive Transformer-based genome language models (gLMs). To answer this question, we adapt AttnLRP, an extension of layer-wise relevance propagation to the attention mechanism, and apply it to the state-of-the-art gLM DNABERT-2. Thereby, we propose strategies to transfer explanations from token and nucleotide level. We evaluate the adaption of AttnLRP on genomic datasets using multiple metrics. Further, we provide an extensive comparison between the explanations of DNABERT-2 and a baseline CNN. Our results demonstrate that AttnLRP yields reliable explanations corresponding to known biological patterns. Hence, like CNNs, gLMs can also help derive biological insights. This work contributes to the explainability of gLMs and addresses the comparability of relevance attributions across different architectures.

AI.tldr: This paper adapts AttnLRP, an extension of layer-wise relevance propagation for attention mechanisms, to the genome language model DNABERT-2, and demonstrates that it produces reliable explanations corresponding to known biological patterns, comparable to CNN-based approaches.
AI.motivation: While CNN explanations have been shown to capture relevant patterns in genome sequences, it is unclear whether this transfers to more expressive Transformer-based genome language models (gLMs). Understanding whether gLMs can provide biologically meaningful explanations is important for biological insight and hypothesis generation.
AI.method: The authors adapt AttnLRP (an extension of layer-wise relevance propagation to attention mechanisms) to the state-of-the-art gLM DNABERT-2. They propose strategies to transfer explanations from token to nucleotide level, evaluate the adaptation on genomic datasets using multiple metrics, and compare explanations between DNABERT-2 and a baseline CNN.
AI.result: AttnLRP yields reliable explanations that correspond to known biological patterns. The results show that, like CNNs, genome language models can also help derive biological insights.
AI.conclusion: This work contributes to the explainability of genome language models and addresses the comparability of relevance attributions across different architectures.

title: Directed walks shape a universal square-root law of entropy production rate in nonreciprocal systems
comment: 9 pages, 2 figures. Supplemental Material submitted for peer review will be made publicly available following peer review
summary: The entropy production rate (EPR) quantifies irreversibility of a nonequilibrium steady state, yet standard formulas obscure how a complex interaction network generates it. For multivariate Ornstein-Uhlenbeck dynamics on such networks, we express the EPR as a quadratic form in antisymmetric matrices measuring the nonreciprocity of aggregate directed walks at every length, and, equivalently, as two weighted-walk quantities: pairs of directed walks sharing both endpoints, and directed closed walks. For diagonalizable interactions, an exact correspondence translates these walk quantities into eigenvalues and biorthogonal eigenvector overlaps. Across dense, sparse, and deep acyclic random interactions satisfying matched-walk conditions, the mean EPR per node universally follows the square-root law $φ_*(g)=1-\sqrt{1-g^2}$, where $g \in [0,1)$ parametrizes the interaction strength. Deep acyclic interaction matrices are nilpotent, with all eigenvalues fixed at zero for every $g$, yet, as their depth increases, their mean EPR per node approaches $φ_*(g)$. Thus, the square-root law arises from directed walk properties, rather than from a shared spectral density or specific network topology.

AI.tldr: The paper derives a new expression for the entropy production rate (EPR) of multivariate Ornstein-Uhlenbeck dynamics on interaction networks, expressing it as a quadratic form in antisymmetric matrices that measure nonreciprocity of directed walks at all lengths. The authors show that across diverse random interaction ensembles (dense, sparse, deep acyclic), the mean EPR per node universally follows a square-root law φ*(g)=1-√(1-g²), arising from directed walk properties rather than spectral or topological features.
AI.motivation: Standard formulas for the entropy production rate in nonequilibrium steady states obscure how complex interaction networks generate irreversible behavior. The authors seek a more transparent decomposition of EPR in terms of network structure, specifically through directed walk properties, to understand what universal features of EPR emerge across different network topologies.
AI.method: The paper analyzes multivariate Ornstein-Uhlenbeck dynamics on interaction networks. EPR is expressed as a quadratic form in antisymmetric matrices measuring the nonreciprocity of aggregate directed walks at every length, and equivalently as weighted-walk quantities involving pairs of directed walks. For diagonalizable interactions, an exact correspondence translates these walk quantities into eigenvalues and biorthogonal eigenvector overlaps. The analysis covers dense, sparse, and deep acyclic random interactions satisfying matched-walk conditions.
AI.result: Across all three classes of random interactions (dense, sparse, and deep acyclic), the mean EPR per node universally follows the square-root law φ*(g)=1-√(1-g²), where g ∈ [0,1) parametrizes interaction strength. Notably, deep acyclic interaction matrices are nilpotent with all eigenvalues zero, yet their mean EPR per node still approaches φ*(g) as depth increases, demonstrating the universality is independent of spectral properties.
AI.conclusion: The square-root law for mean EPR per node arises from directed walk properties rather than from a shared spectral density or specific network topology. This provides a unified understanding of EPR across diverse network structures and reveals that nonreciprocity in directed walks at all lengths is the fundamental mechanism generating irreversibility in these nonequilibrium systems.

title: The Von-Neumann State-Space Transformer for neural decoding
summary: Cortical computation is strikingly low-dimensional: a handful of latent variables, carried in a neural population's activity, steer the higher-dimensional responses of individual neurons. Our aim is sample efficiency-models that decode well from limited data and at small parameter budgets. In a standard Transformer layer, the feed-forward block applies the same operator to every token. We suggest a von-Neumann inspired hypothesis of efficient computation as an alternative for neural decoding: a controller decodes an instruction and then executes a token-specific operator; the usual realization-a soft mixture of experts-only blends their outputs, not operators. We introduce a von-Neumann State-Space Transformer (VN-SST), a memory-augmented Transformer whose feed-forward block is a low-rank instruction bank: a shared base operator plus a small set of learned low-rank instructions, from which a per-token code synthesizes the weight matrix actually used at that token. The code is read from a low- dimensional projection of a carried state-space memory, so a slow latent trajectory acts as an instruction pointer-mirroring how low-dimensional dynamics may route cortical computation. On three motor-cortex neural-decoding benchmarks, VN-SST is far more data-efficient than a modern Transformer, each jointly predicting spikes and decoding behavior. This model wins by a wide margin on the scarcest benchmark, leads on the other two, and turns longer context into rising rather than falling accuracy. We evaluated that the network compresses a large instruction bank to a few bits per token, so program capacity acts as a control channel, not an accuracy lever. The same model is also more parameter-efficient on two small text benchmarks used for language modeling (LLMs), suggesting a generic mechanism.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces VN-SST, a memory-augmented Transformer whose feed-forward block uses a low-rank instruction bank with per-token synthesized weight matrices, guided by low-dimensional state-space memory. It achieves superior data-efficiency on motor-cortex neural decoding benchmarks (especially under scarce data) and also shows parameter-efficiency on small LLM benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Cortical computation is low-dimensional, with a few latent variables steering neural population activity. The authors aim for sample efficiency in neural decoding—models that generalize from limited data and small parameter budgets. Standard Transformer feed-forward blocks apply the same operator to every token, which they argue is suboptimal.
AI.method: VN-SST augments a Transformer with a feed-forward block containing a low-rank instruction bank: a shared base operator plus a small set of learned low-rank instructions. A per-token code (read from a low-dimensional projection of a state-space memory) synthesizes the weight matrix used at each token, acting as an instruction pointer—mirroring low-dimensional dynamics in cortical computation.
AI.result: On three motor-cortex neural-decoding benchmarks, VN-SST is far more data-efficient than a modern Transformer, winning by a wide margin on the scarcest benchmark and leading on the other two. It also converts longer context into rising (not falling) accuracy. The instruction bank compresses to a few bits per token, and the model is more parameter-efficient on two small LLM text benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Program capacity acts as a control channel rather than an accuracy lever, suggesting a generic mechanism: von-Neumann-inspired token-specific operator selection via low-dimensional latent control improves efficiency in both neural decoding and language modeling.

title: Clustering of anterior corneal surface shapes in normal adults
summary: In the present study, we investigated a large dataset of normal adult corneal topographies in an exploratory attempt to identify the natural groupings of their 3D shapes, with the practical clinical aim of categorizing the shape of a future generation of biosynthetic corneal implants. Because of the wide range of shapes among normal corneas, we needed to identify a limited number of normal corneal shape categories to guide the conception of different implants to match the patient's own corneal shape category. At this stage of our research, we focused on the anterior surface, which exhibits greater variation in a normal population and is responsible for most of the refractive power of the eye. The corneal surface 3D data used were the anterior elevation maps taken from corneal topographies. Clustering corneal topography elevation maps was performed to reveal the normal corneal shape categories. To facilitate groupings, corneal data had their dimensionality reduced by Zernike polynomial modeling. The resulting clusters were evaluated using different clustering scores, representations and statistical cluster comparisons. While several hard and soft linear and nonlinear clustering methods were tested in this way, k-means proved to be sufficient for this task. The best number of clusters was three and they were primarily differentiated according to corneal curvature (Zernike defocus coefficient). These clusters were related to established clinical parameters, confirming that the algorithm extracted relevant information based solely on the normal 3D shape of corneas.

AI.tldr: The study analyzed a large dataset of normal adult corneal topographies to identify natural groupings of 3D corneal shapes, with the goal of categorizing shapes for future biosynthetic corneal implants. Using Zernike polynomial dimensionality reduction and clustering methods (with k-means proving sufficient), the best solution yielded three clusters primarily differentiated by corneal curvature (defocus coefficient), which correlated with established clinical parameters.
AI.motivation: Normal corneas exhibit a wide range of shapes, and there is a practical clinical need to categorize these shapes into a limited number of categories to guide the conception of different biosynthetic corneal implants that match each patient's own corneal shape category. The study focuses on the anterior surface because it shows greater variation and is responsible for most of the eye's refractive power.
AI.method: Corneal topography anterior elevation maps were used as 3D surface data. Dimensionality was reduced via Zernike polynomial modeling, followed by clustering of corneal topography elevation maps. Multiple hard and soft linear and nonlinear clustering methods were tested, with k-means proving sufficient. Clusters were evaluated using clustering scores, representations, and statistical cluster comparisons.
AI.result: The optimal number of clusters was three, primarily differentiated according to corneal curvature (Zernike defocus coefficient). These clusters were related to established clinical parameters, confirming that the algorithm extracted relevant information based solely on normal 3D corneal shape.
AI.conclusion: K-means clustering on Zernike-reduced corneal topographic data can identify three meaningful normal corneal shape categories, which may guide the design and selection of biosynthetic corneal implants tailored to individual patients' corneal shapes.

title: Can You Trust Frozen Hematology Foundation Models under Acquisition Shift?
comment: Accepted at the HemaRAI 2026 workshop (MICCAI 2026 satellite event), oral presentation; to appear in MICCAI 2026 Satellite Events, LNCS, Springer. 25 pages (10 main incl. references + 15 supplementary), 4 figures. Project page: https://jaishrm07.github.io/hematology-fm-robustness/
summary: Frozen hematology foundation-model (FM) embeddings reach near-saturated in-domain white-blood-cell (WBC) accuracy, but clinical deployment demands reliability across scanners, sites, stains and preparation pipelines. We audit 15 frozen encoders (hematology, pathology, and general vision) across four public single-cell acquisition domains along two axes: accuracy robustness and calibration. In-domain linear-probe macro-F1 is saturated (0.98-0.997), yet cross-dataset macro-F1 drops 34-72% and rankings re-order: DinoBloom-L, the in-domain best, falls to 10th of 15 on the most-shifted target (MLL23) at the benchmark's shared 224-px input, behind RedDino and several general and pathology encoders. Rank transfer is probe-dependent: 1-NN retrieval is more stable on average than a source-fitted linear head (median $ρ$ 0.65 vs 0.45), but neither probe universally predicts target robustness. Calibration also collapses: source-trained probes are nearly calibrated in-domain (expected calibration error, ECE, 0.004) but confidently wrong off-domain (ECE 0.35), and source-fitted temperature scaling transfers poorly. We further audit pretraining exposure and identify MLL23 as DinoBloom's internal cohort; because DinoBloom's only held-out dataset is also our source domain, this benchmark cannot isolate exposure from scanner-associated shift. Label-free adaptation and marginal-entropy-based model selection appear safe under balanced evaluation but fail under realistic WBC class-prior shift. Class-Balanced Re-standardization (CBR), a training-free pseudo-label-balanced feature normalization, improves all evaluated target-prior scenario means and partially improves calibration, although encoder-level exceptions and residual miscalibration remain. Hematology FM benchmarks must therefore jointly audit accuracy, calibration, exposure, and class-prior robustness.

AI.tldr: This paper audits 15 frozen foundation-model encoders for white-blood-cell classification across four public datasets, finding that in-domain accuracy is saturated but cross-dataset accuracy drops 34-72% and calibration collapses. The in-domain best model (DinoBloom-L) falls to 10th of 15 on the most shifted target, and the benchmark itself has a data-exposure confound (DinoBloom's internal cohort is MLL23). The authors propose Class-Balanced Re-standardization (CBR), a training-free pseudo-label-balanced feature normalization that partially improves both accuracy and calibration under class-prior shift.
AI.motivation: Frozen hematology foundation-model embeddings achieve near-saturated in-domain accuracy, but clinical deployment requires reliability across diverse scanners, sites, stains, and preparation pipelines—a robustness property that current benchmarks fail to assess adequately.
AI.method: The authors audit 15 frozen encoders (hematology, pathology, and general vision) across four public single-cell acquisition domains along two axes: accuracy robustness and calibration. They assess linear-probe and 1-NN retrieval rank transfer, calibration error, pretraining data exposure, label-free adaptation, marginal-entropy model selection, and propose Class-Balanced Re-standardization (CBR), a training-free pseudo-label-balanced feature normalization technique.
AI.result: In-domain macro-F1 is saturated (0.98-0.997) but cross-dataset macro-F1 drops 34-72% with rank re-ordering. Calibration collapses from ECE 0.004 in-domain to 0.35 off-domain. The benchmark has a contamination issue: MLL23 is DinoBloom's internal cohort. CBR improves all evaluated target-prior scenario means and partially improves calibration, though encoder-level exceptions and residual miscalibration persist.
AI.conclusion: Hematology foundation-model benchmarks must jointly audit accuracy, calibration, exposure, and class-prior robustness, as linear-probe performance alone is misleading and current evaluation practices are confounded by data exposure and class-prior assumptions.

title: Federation Is Nearly Free, Reasoning Is Not: Tradeoffs for AI Co-Scientists in Protein Characterization Workflows
comment: 24 Pages, 4 main figures, 5 main tables, 2 supplementary figures
summary: Natural language driven autonomous co-scientist workflows involve a fundamental trade-off between flexibility and reasoning at the expense of determinism, reproducibility, and observability. Such agents increasingly must communicate across institutional boundaries, where federation topology can shape latency and cost. We systematically evaluated these tradeoffs using a controlled ablation on a production agentic platform for science. We use a verifiable task: given a protein sequence, we ask an agent to confidently characterize its function by routing across common tools. We compare federation topology, classic RL vs LLM-driven harnesses, language model, and prompt expertise. We also stratify results by protein novelty. We find that the choice of LLM dominated prediction quality far more than topology or prompting (Opus ~92%-94% vs o4-mini ~40%-50%). The PPO policy was nearly as accurate as the best LLM (88%) at zero token cost, fastest latency, and perfect consistency, but yields no reasoning trace. Expert prompted LLMs reached the highest accuracy but were high-cost and less consistent; prompt dependence was largest when the task was hardest. Federation imposed a negligible penalty on performance. These results offer actionable guidance for deploying agents for scientific workflows: for routine, verifiable tasks, a cheap deterministic policy delivers near-frontier accuracy with complete reproducibility, while flexible LLM reasoning is best reserved for open-ended discovery.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically evaluates trade-offs in natural language driven autonomous co-scientist workflows, comparing federation topology, RL vs LLM-driven harnesses, LLM choice, and prompt expertise on a verifiable protein function characterization task. Results show LLM choice dominates performance (Opus ~92-94% vs o4-mini ~40-50%), PPO policy achieves near-frontier accuracy (88%) at zero cost with perfect consistency but no reasoning trace, and federation imposes negligible penalty.
AI.motivation: Autonomous scientific agents face a fundamental tension between flexibility and reasoning versus determinism, reproducibility, and observability. As these agents increasingly operate across institutional boundaries where federation topology impacts latency and cost, there is a need to systematically understand these trade-offs to guide deployment decisions.
AI.method: Controlled ablation on a production agentic platform for science using a verifiable task: given a protein sequence, agents must confidently characterize its function by routing across common tools. Comparisons include federation topology, classic RL (PPO) vs LLM-driven harnesses, language model selection, and prompt expertise, with results stratified by protein novelty.
AI.result: LLM choice dominated prediction quality (Opus ~92-94% vs o4-mini ~40-50%). PPO policy achieved ~88% accuracy at zero token cost with fastest latency and perfect consistency but no reasoning trace. Expert-prompted LLMs reached highest accuracy but were high-cost and less consistent, with prompt dependence largest on hardest tasks. Federation imposed negligible performance penalty.
AI.conclusion: For routine verifiable tasks, a cheap deterministic policy (PPO) delivers near-frontier accuracy with complete reproducibility, while flexible LLM reasoning is best reserved for open-ended discovery tasks. These findings provide actionable guidance for deploying agents in scientific workflows.

title: BixBench3: Benchmarking AI agents on research-study-scale computational biology tasks
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) promises to accelerate biological research by automating computational analyses. Yet the ability of AI agents to carry out computational biology at the scale of complete research studies has not been systematically evaluated. Here we introduce BixBench3, a benchmark that measures the capacity of AI agents to process raw biological data through to scientific results. We designed BixBench3 tasks to mirror the delegation of work from a scientist to an agent: the scientist chooses the research question and high-level methods, then delegates implementation of all analyses to the agent. In each task, an agent receives a research objective, methodological guidance, and raw data derived from a published scientific study, and must execute a sequence of analyses to achieve the research objective. The data artifacts resulting from these analyses - such as peak call matrices or differential expression tables - are programmatically graded against the corresponding artifacts generated and reported in the original study. Across 20 BixBench3 tasks encompassing the generation of 138 unique artifacts, we find that 13 frontier models achieve scores ranging from 0.00 for Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite to 0.48 for GPT 5.6 Sol. Agents perform worse on tasks with larger raw datasets (0.36 on tasks with <100 GB versus 0.10 on tasks with >100 GB) and on analyses requiring more sequential steps (0.36 at 1-2 steps vs 0.24 at 3+). On average, agents use 6.8 hours, 102 million tokens, and $43 to complete each task, with the longest attempts consuming 24 hours, 1.07 billion tokens, and $525. Notably, the highest-scoring agents used fewer tokens and were cheaper than less performant options. These results reveal that LLMs vary substantially in their ability to (1) execute multiple sequential analysis steps coherently, (2) manage large quantities of raw data, and (3) work across scientific domains.

AI.tldr: BixBench3 is a benchmark evaluating AI agents' ability to perform complete computational biology research studies, from raw data processing to scientific results. Across 20 tasks and 13 frontier models, best scores reach only 0.48 (GPT 5.6 Sol), with performance degrading on large datasets and multi-step analyses. Agents average 6.8 hours and $43 per task.
AI.motivation: While AI promises to accelerate biological research through automation, there is no systematic evaluation of whether AI agents can carry out complete computational biology studies end-to-end—from raw data to publishable results—rather than just isolated analyses.
AI.method: BixBench3 presents 20 tasks derived from published studies where agents receive a research objective, methodological guidance, and raw data. Agents must execute a sequence of analyses producing artifacts (e.g., peak call matrices, differential expression tables) that are programmatically graded against the original study's outputs. Thirteen frontier models were evaluated with varying dataset sizes and task complexity.
AI.result: Frontier models scored from 0.00 (Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite) to 0.48 (GPT 5.6 Sol). Performance dropped on large datasets (0.36 for <100 GB vs 0.10 for >100 GB) and on tasks requiring more sequential steps (0.36 at 1-2 steps vs 0.24 at 3+). Agents averaged 6.8 hours, 102M tokens, and $43 per task. Higher-scoring agents were more token-efficient and cheaper.
AI.conclusion: LLMs vary substantially in their ability to execute coherent multi-step analyses, manage large raw datasets, and work across scientific domains—highlighting key bottlenecks that must be addressed before AI agents can reliably conduct end-to-end biological research.

title: Interpreting Protein Language Model Embeddings via Orthogonal Projection for Protein Fitness Prediction
summary: Recently, there has been a growing adoption of protein language models (PLMs) in biomedical science. Their embeddings provide a rich numerical representation of protein sequences which achieve state-of-the-art performance on several downstream tasks including protein fitness prediction. However, PLM embeddings are not directly interpretable and, thereby, it remains unclear what features they encode. To gain insight into which biochemical properties of the protein are driving the prediction, we leverage an orthogonal projection technique that removes linear effects of known tabular features from embeddings and extend it to high-order and interaction effects. In this way, we remove the effects of interpretable biochemical features from PLM embeddings. In an ablation study, we show that this leads to a decrease in performance for a downstream classifier trained only on the embeddings to predict protein fitness. In an additional evaluation, we find that these biochemical features explain a substantial part of the variance in the predictions of this classifier. Hence, we can show that PLM embeddings encode patterns correlated with biochemical properties and quantify their contribution to predicting protein fitness. This computationally efficient approach is not limited to the features or embeddings considered here and is readily transferable to problem settings beyond protein fitness prediction.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes protein language model (PLM) embeddings to determine which biochemical properties they encode, using an orthogonal projection technique that removes linear, high-order, and interaction effects of interpretable tabular biochemical features. Through ablation studies on protein fitness prediction, they show performance drops when these features are removed, demonstrating that PLM embeddings encode biochemical properties and quantifying their contribution to fitness prediction.
AI.motivation: While PLM embeddings achieve state-of-the-art performance on downstream tasks like protein fitness prediction, they are not directly interpretable. It remains unclear what biological/biochemical features are encoded within these embeddings, which hinders understanding of what drives predictions.
AI.method: The authors extend an orthogonal projection technique to remove linear, high-order, and interaction effects of known interpretable biochemical tabular features from PLM embeddings. They then train a downstream classifier on the modified embeddings for protein fitness prediction and evaluate performance degradation in an ablation study, while also quantifying the variance explained by the removed biochemical features.
AI.result: Removing biochemical feature effects from PLM embeddings leads to a decrease in downstream classifier performance for protein fitness prediction, and the biochemical features explain a substantial portion of the variance in the classifier's predictions, confirming that PLM embeddings encode patterns correlated with biochemical properties.
AI.conclusion: PLM embeddings encode biochemical properties that meaningfully contribute to protein fitness prediction, and the proposed computationally efficient orthogonal projection approach is generalizable beyond fitness prediction and the specific features/embeddings studied, offering a transferable interpretability tool for PLM-based analyses.

title: Giant strongly biconnected components of directed networks: a generating function approach
summary: Strongly connected components (SCCs) characterize modular structure in directed networks but are fragile to single node failures. We study strongly biconnected components (SBCs), which are the set of nodes in which every node pair remains mutually reachable after the removal of any single node, as a more robust notion of connectivity. Using a generating function formalism, we derive the size of the giant SBC and analyze its percolation behavior under random node and link removal. We show that the giant SBC emerges at the same threshold as the giant SCC but grows more slowly due to stricter connectivity requirements. We also applied our theoretical framework to real-world biological networks including gene regulatory networks and neural connectome. Our framework provides insight into the interplay between connectivity, redundancy, and robustness in complex directed systems.

AI.tldr: This paper studies strongly biconnected components (SBCs) in directed networks—sets of nodes where every pair remains mutually reachable even after any single node is removed—as a more robust connectivity measure than standard SCCs. Using generating function formalism, the authors derive the size of the giant SBC and analyze its percolation behavior under random node and link removal, finding it emerges at the same threshold as the giant SCC but grows more slowly. The framework is applied to real-world biological networks including gene regulatory networks and neural connectomes.
AI.motivation: Strongly connected components (SCCs) capture modular structure in directed networks but are fragile to single node failures. A more robust notion of connectivity is needed to characterize network resilience, motivating the study of strongly biconnected components (SBCs) where every node pair remains mutually reachable after any single node removal.
AI.method: The authors use a generating function formalism to derive the size of the giant SBC in directed networks and analyze its percolation behavior under random node and link removal.
AI.result: The giant SBC emerges at the same percolation threshold as the giant SCC but grows more slowly due to stricter connectivity requirements. The theoretical framework was successfully applied to real-world biological networks including gene regulatory networks and neural connectomes.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides insight into the interplay between connectivity, redundancy, and robustness in complex directed systems, offering a more resilient connectivity measure for analyzing modular structure in directed networks.

title: GenAIT: Development and Validation of an Objective Generative AI Literacy Test for High School Students
summary: There is growing international interest in generative AI (GenAI) literacy and its assessment among high school students, but objective assessment in this population remains underdeveloped. This article reports the iterative development and validation of the GenAI Literacy Test (GenAIT), an 18-item multiple-choice test measuring high school students' conceptual knowledge about GenAI, with content spanning technical, practical, and human-impact domains. Expert review of relevance, clarity, and comprehensiveness provided evidence of content validity. In a large-scale survey of 7432 Estonian high school students, we evaluated the psychometric functioning of the Estonian-language GenAIT using confirmatory factor analysis, classical test theory, and item response theory. Results supported approximate unidimensionality, broadly adequate reliability for group-level research (marginal reliability = .72, KR-20 = .69), and good fit of a three-parameter logistic model (RMSEA = .013, TLI = .987, CFI = .990, SRMSR = .021). Measurement precision was sufficient for the majority of students but varied substantially across the latent trait, with lower precision for lower scoring students. GenAIT is therefore more suitable for group-level research than high-stakes individual classification. GenAIT scores were unrelated to perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use, and negatively associated with LLM use frequency, suggesting that frequent use and favorable perceptions of AI should not be treated as proxies for conceptual understanding.

AI.tldr: This paper reports the iterative development and validation of the GenAI Literacy Test (GenAIT), an 18-item multiple-choice test for high school students measuring conceptual knowledge about GenAI across technical, practical, and human-impact domains. Validation with 7,432 Estonian students supported approximate unidimensionality, adequate group-level reliability, and good model fit, though measurement precision was lower for lower-scoring students. Notably, GenAIT scores were unrelated to perceived usefulness/ease of use and negatively associated with LLM use frequency, indicating that AI usage and favorable perceptions are not proxies for conceptual understanding.
AI.motivation: There is growing international interest in GenAI literacy assessment among high school students, but objective assessment tools for this population are underdeveloped. Researchers sought to fill this gap by creating a validated, objective measure of conceptual knowledge about GenAI.
AI.method: The authors iteratively developed an 18-item multiple-choice test (GenAIT) spanning technical, practical, and human-impact domains. They established content validity through expert review, then administered the test to 7,432 Estonian high school students and evaluated psychometric properties using confirmatory factor analysis, classical test theory, and item response theory (three-parameter logistic model).
AI.result: The test showed approximate unidimensionality, adequate group-level reliability (marginal reliability = .72; KR-20 = .69), and good model fit (RMSEA = .013, TLI = .987, CFI = .990, SRMSR = .021). Measurement precision was sufficient for most students but varied across the latent trait with lower precision for lower-scoring students. Scores were unrelated to perceived usefulness/ease of use and negatively associated with LLM use frequency.
AI.conclusion: GenAIT is suitable for group-level research rather than high-stakes individual classification. The findings caution against using AI usage frequency or favorable perceptions of AI as proxies for genuine conceptual understanding of GenAI.

title: CardioFusion-AI: Robust ECG--PPG Fusion for Multimodal Physiological Monitoring Under Signal Degradation
comment: 7 pages, 4 figures. Under review at IEEE Journal of Biomedical and Health Informatics. Code: https://github.com/ka-cyber/CardioFusion-AI
summary: Wearable electrocardiogram (ECG) and photoplethysmogram (PPG) sensors are complementary but individually fragile: motion artifact, poor contact, and sensor dropout can degrade one or both signals. Fusion strategies that assume both modalities are equally trustworthy can become less reliable than a single clean modality under degradation. We present CardioFusion-AI, a framework whose signal-processing front end, including R-peak and systolic-peak detection, an Orphanidou-type signal-quality index, and beat-by-beat pulse transit time estimation, is validated on 53 real intensive-care recordings (848 windows; heart-rate mean absolute error 1.61 bpm for ECG and 2.78 bpm for PPG) and a real annotated fetal ECG database (R-peak F1 0.89-0.98). We then conduct a controlled synthetic degradation study comparing eight ECG-PPG fusion strategies across six degradation regimes spanning graded corruption and complete modality loss, using five independent training seeds. Attention fusion achieved the lowest descriptive overall error (1.66+/-0.43 bpm). Both adaptive gates reallocated weight toward the healthy modality under complete modality loss, but showed near-zero correlation between gate weight and signal quality under graded degradation (r = 0.10-0.24). Signal-quality conditioning produced a specific improvement under missing-PPG conditions (1.56+/-0.59 bpm), approaching the 1.48 bpm unimodal ceiling. With only five training seeds, no pairwise comparison survives Holm-corrected significance testing; effect sizes and confidence intervals are therefore reported. These results indicate that modality availability and modality quality are functionally distinct problems for adaptive fusion.

AI.tldr: CardioFusion-AI is a fusion framework for wearable ECG and PPG signals that validates signal-processing front ends on real clinical data and systematically compares eight fusion strategies under controlled synthetic degradation, finding that attention fusion performs best overall but that adaptive gates fail to track signal quality under graded degradation—revealing that modality availability and modality quality are functionally distinct problems.
AI.motivation: Wearable ECG and PPG sensors are individually fragile under motion artifact, poor contact, and dropout. Existing fusion strategies assume both modalities are equally trustworthy, which can degrade performance below that of a single clean modality. A systematic understanding of how to fuse these complementary but unreliable signals under degradation is needed.
AI.method: The framework includes a signal-processing front end (R-peak and systolic-peak detection, Orphanidou-type SQI, beat-by-beat pulse transit time estimation) validated on 53 real ICU recordings (848 windows) and a fetal ECG database. A controlled synthetic degradation study then compares eight ECG-PPG fusion strategies across six degradation regimes with five training seeds, including attention fusion, adaptive gates, and signal-quality conditioning.
AI.result: Front end achieved 1.61 bpm MAE for ECG and 2.78 bpm for PPG; R-peak F1 0.89-0.98 on fetal ECG. Attention fusion had the lowest overall error (1.66±0.43 bpm). Adaptive gates reallocated weight under complete modality loss but showed near-zero correlation with signal quality under graded degradation (r=0.10-0.24). Signal-quality conditioning improved missing-PPG conditions (1.56±0.59 bpm), approaching the 1.48 bpm unimodal ceiling. No pairwise comparison survived Holm-corrected significance testing with only five seeds.
AI.conclusion: Modality availability and modality quality are functionally distinct problems for adaptive fusion. Signal-quality conditioning helps under complete modality loss but adaptive gates fail to respond to graded degradation. Reported effect sizes and confidence intervals provide evidence despite limited statistical power.
